claims.claim: A hand-held fan blown at the face reduced breathlessness compared with the fan on the legs.
claims.supporting_passage: Fifty participants were randomized to use a handheld fan for five minutes directed to their face or leg first and then crossed over to the other treatment. ... There was a significant difference in the VAS scores between the two treatments, with a reduction in breathlessness when the fan was directed to the face (P=0.003).
claims.pico_timeframe: 50 adults with advanced disease / fan to face 5 min / fan to legs / breathlessness VAS / immediate
claims.safe_wording: In a small trial of 50 people with advanced illness, five minutes of a hand-held fan blowing on the face eased breathlessness more than the same fan blowing on the legs.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Longer-term benefit not shown by this trial.

claims.claim: In people without low oxygen levels, oxygen through nasal tubes gave no more relief than room air; both groups improved.
claims.supporting_passage: From baseline to day 6, mean morning breathlessness changed by -0.9 points (95% CI -1.3 to -0.5) in patients assigned to receive oxygen and by -0.7 points (-1.2 to -0.2) in patients assigned to receive room air (p=0.504). ... Since oxygen delivered by a nasal cannula provides no additional symptomatic benefit for relief of refractory dyspnoea in patients with life-limiting illness compared with room air, less burdensome strategies should be considered after brief assessment of the effect of oxygen therapy on the individual patient.
claims.pico_timeframe: 239 outpatients, life-limiting illness, PaO2 >7.3 kPa / oxygen 2 L/min via nasal cannula / room air via same concentrator / breathlessness 0-10 / 7 days
claims.safe_wording: In a trial of 239 people with serious illness whose blood oxygen was not low, oxygen through nasal tubes eased breathlessness no more than room air given through the same tubes; both groups felt a little better.
claims.qualifications: Excluded people with low blood oxygen; outpatients, not dying people; 7 days.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Improvement in both groups may reflect air flow, expectation or natural course; the trial cannot separate these.

numbers.meaning: mean change in morning breathlessness (0-10 scale) day 6, oxygen vs room air, p=0.504

claims.claim: In 32 people near death, oxygen, medical air and no flow made no difference to observed respiratory distress; 91% tolerated the protocol.
claims.supporting_passage: Most (91%) patients tolerated the protocol with no change in respiratory comfort. Three patients (9%) displayed distress and were restored to baseline oxygen ... Repeated-measure analysis of variance revealed no differences in the Respiratory Distress Observation Scale under changing gas and flow conditions. ... The n-of-1 trial of oxygen in clinical practice is appropriate in the face of hypoxemic respiratory distress.
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients near death without baseline distress / oxygen, air, no flow alternated every 10 min / observer-rated distress
claims.safe_wording: In a small study of people close to death who were not in distress, switching between oxygen, air and no flow made no difference to breathing distress for most; 3 of 32 became distressed and went back on oxygen.
claims.qualifications: Small; people not distressed at start; distress rated by observers.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The same study supports trying oxygen for an individual with low oxygen and distress.

numbers.meaning: of 32 patients tolerated with no change
showed distress and returned to oxygen

claims.claim: Oxygen can cause nasal irritation and add cost.
claims.supporting_passage: Campbell (background): "Oxygen may produce nasal irritation and increase the cost of care." Abernethy: "The frequency of side-effects did not differ between groups."
claims.safe_wording: Oxygen tubing and equipment are a burden for some people; the post should not claim trial-proven extra side-effects.
claims.qualifications: Campbell's statement is background, not a finding. In Abernethy nasal irritation was not more common with oxygen than air through the same tubes.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Abernethy found no difference in side-effects.

claims.claim: The noise is presumed to come from secretions gathering in the airways that the dying person cannot clear.
claims.supporting_passage: Cochrane: "The cause of death rattle remains unproven but is presumed to be due to an accumulation of secretions in the airways. It is therefore managed physically (repositioning and clearing the upper airways of fluid with a mechanical sucker) or pharmacologically (with anticholinergic drugs)." SILENCE: "Death rattle, defined as noisy breathing caused by the presence of mucus in the respiratory tract, is relatively common among dying patients."
claims.safe_wording: The rattling sound is thought to come from saliva and mucus collecting in the throat and airways when a dying person can no longer cough or swallow it away.

claims.claim: The person is thought not to be distressed by the sound.
claims.supporting_passage: The impact of death rattle on patients was less well described, although there was a consensus that death rattle is not distressing to affected patients (but may be distressing to other patients).
claims.safe_wording: Experts generally agree the sound is unlikely to distress the dying person, but this has not been measured well.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Further research on patients' experience called for.

claims.claim: Some relatives are distressed by the sound, especially if they think the person is choking or drowning; others are not.
claims.supporting_passage: Wee II: "Seventeen of the 25 bereaved relatives interviewed had heard the sound of death rattle. Ten relatives were distressed by the sound, but seven were not. Some relatives regarded the sound of death rattle as a useful warning sign that death was imminent. ... Relatives were distressed when they thought that the sound of death rattle indicated that the patient might be drowning or choking." Wee I: "almost half of the 12 relatives who had heard the sound of death rattle had been distressed by it. The others were either neutral about the sound or found it a helpful signal of impending death." Fagan 2025: "related distress was common amongst informal carers".
claims.safe_wording: In interview studies, some relatives were upset by the sound, especially when they thought the person was choking or drowning; others were not, and some took it as a sign that death was close.
claims.qualifications: Small qualitative studies; Wee I abstract says 'almost half of the 12' (the 5 of 12 figure is from Wee II's summary of study I).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A Dutch interview study (van Esch 2020) found most relatives distressed and that information alone did not always ease it.

numbers.meaning: relatives who heard the sound and were distressed (Wee II)
Wee I, as reported in Wee II abstract

claims.claim: Repositioning is a recognised way to manage the sound; evidence that any treatment helps an established rattle is lacking.
claims.supporting_passage: It is therefore managed physically (repositioning and clearing the upper airways of fluid with a mechanical sucker) or pharmacologically (with anticholinergic drugs). ... There is currently no evidence to show that any intervention, be it pharmacological or non-pharmacological, is superior to placebo in the treatment of death rattle. ... relatives need time, explanation and reassurance to relieve their fears and concerns.
claims.safe_wording: Changing the person's position is a common first step; there is little trial evidence that medicines or other measures quiet the sound once it has started. Relatives need time and explanation.
claims.qualifications: Do not claim repositioning is proven to reduce the sound. Review is from 2008.

claims.claim: A preventive injection of hyoscine butylbromide reduced death rattle from 27% to 13% in Dutch hospices.
claims.supporting_passage: A death rattle occurred in 10 patients (13%) in the scopolamine group compared with 21 patients (27%) in the placebo group (difference, 14%; 95% CI, 2%-27%, P = .02).
claims.pico_timeframe: 157 dying hospice patients / scopolamine butylbromide 20 mg SC four times daily from recognition of dying / placebo / grade 2+ rattle
claims.safe_wording: In a Dutch hospice trial, giving hyoscine butylbromide as soon as dying was recognised, before any rattle, meant about 13 in 100 developed the rattle compared with 27 in 100 on placebo.
claims.qualifications: Prevention, not treatment of an established rattle; hospice setting; restlessness 28% vs 23%.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Whether prevention is worthwhile is debated (van Esch 2023 controversies article).

numbers.meaning: rattle occurrence, drug vs placebo, absolute difference 14 percentage points

claims.claim: Abrupt stopping of Parkinson's medicines can rarely cause parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, a dangerous condition resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
claims.supporting_passage: Beckers 2025 (full text, Introduction): "In rare cases, acute cessation causes parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome. This potentially life-limiting syndrome is a specific form of neuroleptic malignant syndrome and consists of severe rigidity, autonomic dysfunction (e.g., hyperthermia, tachycardia), rhabdomyolysis and disturbances of consciousness." And: "Acute cessation of levodopa might result in a severe relapse of PD symptoms ... This includes a worsening of motor symptoms, such as akinesia, rigidity or tremor, and also of non-motor symptoms, such as anxiety and pain." End-of-life section: "If a person has sufficient symptom control with palliative treatments, including palliative sedation, one can opt to omit dopaminergic treatment altogether – although sudden cessation carries a risk of parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome." Also: "In the 72 h before death, severe motor symptoms were present in only 6% of persons in one study." Wang 2022 abstract (retained): "...caused by abrupt withdrawal of antiparkinsonian medication."
claims.location: Beckers: Introduction; 'Unplanned cessation ... at the end of life'. Wang: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Case reports and review of 56 cases
claims.safe_wording: Stopping Parkinson's medicines suddenly can bring severe stiffness, pain and anxiety, and in rare cases a dangerous reaction with high fever. At the end of life, some people have good symptom control without them, so the decision is individual: ask what is making the person uncomfortable, and decide on purpose rather than by default.
claims.qualifications: Withdrawal syndrome is rare. Expert review, not trial evidence. Reviewers note that tapering off dopaminergic medicine may be possible with limited harm in some people; terminal stiffness was documented in only 3 of 51 people in the 72 hours before death (Wilson 2024) and 6% in one study cited by Beckers. The post must not say that stopping is always harmful.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Several experts argue dopaminergic medicine can be tapered at the end of life with limited negative consequences; others continue it until death. Frequency of the withdrawal syndrome near death is unknown.

claims.claim: A rotigotine skin patch is commonly used when oral Parkinson's medicines can no longer be swallowed at the end of life; conversion is approximate.
claims.supporting_passage: Hindmarsh: "when oral administration of antiparkinsonian medications is no longer possible in dying patients, it is becoming common place to initiate transdermal rotigotine, despite a paucity of evidence to guide dosing. ... The majority of patients were converted to transdermal rotigotine (90%). Patients converted to a higher than equivalent dose of rotigotine were more likely to be agitated (p < 0.05)" Ibrahim: "25 (30%) patients were prescribed the recommended dose of Rotigotine; 31 (37%) higher and 28 (33%) lower than recommended. ... Inappropriate dosing may precipitate or worsen delirium/hallucinations. Use at end-of-life requires further evaluation." || Beckers 2025: "Based on these studies, transdermal rotigotine is the most widely used non-oral strategy at the end of life. In a UK-based cohort of 51 PwP at the end-of-life, 55% had dopaminergic medication substituted with transdermal rotigotine at death. However, evidence regarding its effectiveness is scarce" and "The equivalency factor from levodopa to transdermal rotigotine is 30:1 and the maximum dose of rotigotine is 16 mg/24 h, corresponding to 480 mg levodopa." and "it can sometimes induce psychotic symptoms or worsen autonomic symptoms" and "as many as 24% of subjects developed a delirium" (in a study of people with advanced PD started on a rotigotine patch). || Hewer 2024 abstract: "83% (n = 52) of PWP were eligible for rotigotine and, of those, 13% (n = 7) received the correct dose, 38% (n = 20) a lower dose, 12% (n = 6) a higher dose and 37% (n = 19) did not receive any. ... Rotigotine dose and admission LEDD were both associated with proxy measures of distress in the last 72 hours of life. This suggests cautious use of rotigotine at EOL." || Kim 2023 abstract: "Although rotigotine patch and apormorphine injections are most frequently recommended, there are no clinical trials in this patient population to support those recommendations."
claims.location: Beckers: 'Unplanned cessation ... at the end of life' and Table 1; Hewer, Kim: Abstracts
claims.pico_timeframe: UK hospital inpatients with Parkinson's, retrospective
claims.safe_wording: When a person with Parkinson's can no longer swallow, a rotigotine skin patch is the most widely used non-oral option near the end of life, but no trials show it works there. Doses are approximate (about 30 mg of levodopa to 1 mg of rotigotine), the patch cannot replace high levodopa doses, and too high a dose is linked with confusion, hallucinations and agitation. In one Australian hospital, only 7 of 52 eligible people got the recommended dose. Agree the dose with pharmacy or the Parkinson's team.
claims.qualifications: Observational and expert-opinion evidence only. Absorption through skin can be reduced by sweating, weight loss and poor circulation. Apomorphine and subcutaneous levodopa are other non-oral routes but need specialist set-up and may be unavailable. Use the conversion ratio only if the practitioner audience is the target and label it approximate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Case reports conflict (two improved, two had insufficient effect). Hindmarsh found lower-than-equivalent doses possibly better tolerated. Rotigotine dose was associated with more benzodiazepine use in the last 72 hours (Hewer).

numbers.meaning: levodopa to rotigotine equivalence factor; maximum rotigotine 16 mg/24 h corresponds to 480 mg levodopa (Beckers)
eligible people given the correct rotigotine dose in the last 72 hours of life, one Australian hospital (Hewer)
patches prescribed at the recommended dose, UK teaching hospital (Ibrahim)
of 100 dying inpatients converted to rotigotine (Hindmarsh)
UK cohort with dopaminergic medicine substituted with rotigotine at death (quoted by Beckers)

claims.claim: Dopamine-blocking medicines (for example metoclopramide and haloperidol) are contraindicated in Parkinson's disease, including near the end of life, and are still prescribed.
claims.supporting_passage: Hewer 2024 abstract: "Contraindicated dopamine antagonists were prescribed for 43% of PWP and administered in 31% of those cases." || Beckers 2025 (full text, surgery section): "certain drugs which are commonly used periprocedurally are contraindicated in PwP (examples include ketamine, metoclopramide and haloperidol)." || Lertxundi 2017 abstract: "...the administration of centrally acting antidopaminergics. ... inappropriate antiemetic administration OR = 2.15 CI 95% (1.36-3.39); and inappropriate antipsychotic administration OR = 1.91 ... Inappropriately omitted doses and both inappropriate antipsychotic and antiemetic administration were associated with a significant 4-day increase in median hospital stay."
claims.location: Hewer: Abstract (Results). Beckers: Surgery section. Lertxundi: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: 1628 PD inpatients, Spain / antidopaminergic drugs / none / mortality, LOS
claims.safe_wording: Metoclopramide and haloperidol block dopamine and are listed as contraindicated in Parkinson's disease. In an Australian audit of people with Parkinson's who died in hospital, 43% were prescribed a contraindicated dopamine blocker and 31% of those prescriptions were given. Check every anti-sickness, calming and sedative medicine on the chart against its dopamine-blocking effect.
claims.qualifications: Beckers names metoclopramide and haloperidol (with ketamine) in a perioperative context, not specifically for the last days of life; the Hewer audit is end-of-life but its abstract does not list the drugs. Do not name safe alternatives or other drugs (for example levomepromazine, prochlorperazine) as unsafe or safe: not verified from an opened source. NICE NG71 and Scottish guideline text could not be opened. Lertxundi is observational and not end-of-life specific.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Beckers notes opioids and benzodiazepines, otherwise best avoided in earlier disease, are the mainstay at the end of life; and for confusion lorazepam or midazolam subcutaneously are suggested. Guideline-level list of dopamine-blocking drugs to avoid not verified.

numbers.meaning: of people with Parkinson's who died at one Australian hospital were prescribed a contraindicated dopamine antagonist (Hewer; denominator about 63 people, check full text before using)

claims.claim: About 1 in 10 bereaved adults develop prolonged grief disorder after non-violent loss; higher mean age linked with higher prevalence.
claims.supporting_passage: Meta-analysis revealed a pooled prevalence of PGD of 9.8% (95% CI 6.8-14.0). Moderation analyses showed higher mean age to be associated with higher prevalence of PGD. ... Due to heterogeneity and limited representativeness, the findings should be interpreted cautiously
claims.safe_wording: Studies suggest roughly 1 in 10 adults bereaved by a non-violent death develop grief that stays intense and disabling; it appears more common in older groups.
claims.qualifications: Heterogeneous studies, pre-ICD-11 criteria; age link is across studies.

claims.claim: In adults 50+, complicated grief treatment gave a response rate of 70.5% vs 32.0% with interpersonal psychotherapy.
claims.supporting_passage: Response rate for CGT (52 individuals [70.5%]) was more than twice that for IPT (24 [32.0%]) (relative risk, 2.20 [95% CI, 1.51-3.22]; P < .001), with the number needed to treat at 2.56. ... Results were not moderated by participant age.
claims.pico_timeframe: 151 adults 50+ (mean 66), New York / 16 sessions CGT / grief-focused IPT / response at 20 weeks
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial of 151 people aged 50 and over, about 7 in 10 improved with a grief-specific therapy, compared with about 3 in 10 with a talking therapy proven for depression.
claims.qualifications: One US trial; comparator is an active therapy.

claims.claim: ICD-11 includes prolonged grief disorder with a 6-month criterion.
claims.safe_wording: Do not state the ICD-11 duration unless verified; may say it was 'expected to be included in ICD-11' (Lundorff 2017).

claims.claim: Guidance sets the as-needed opioid dose at one sixth (or one tenth to one sixth) of the 24-hour dose and advises recalculating when the regular dose changes.
claims.qualifications: Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines, PCF and EAPC text not opened in this batch.

candidates.reason: All claims supported by abstracts; C19-21-d must be softened (side-effects not higher with oxygen in trial).
Supported with qualifications: patient comfort is consensus not measurement; repositioning is practice not proven; SILENCE is prevention.

Withdrawal risk, rotigotine as the most widely used non-oral route (with scarce effectiveness evidence and approximate dosing), and dopamine blockers contraindicated (metoclopramide, haloperidol named in an opened full text; 43% prescribed in an Australian end-of-life audit) are now supported by an opened full-text practice review plus abstracts. The editor's position 'convert, not simply stop' is stronger than the evidence: the review says some people do well with tapering and omission when comfort is controlled. NICE NG71 and Scottish guideline text not opened; no named safe alternatives.
candidates.revised_angle: Teaching round: 'stop all oral medicines' is a decision, not a default, for a person with Parkinson's who can no longer swallow. Sudden withdrawal can bring severe stiffness, pain and anxiety and, rarely, a dangerous fever reaction. Ask what is causing discomfort and decide on purpose. A rotigotine patch is the most widely used non-oral route (no trial evidence; dose approximate and agreed with pharmacy or the Parkinson's team; too high a dose is linked with confusion and agitation). Whatever is chosen, check the chart for dopamine-blocking medicines (metoclopramide, haloperidol named), which are contraindicated. Do not name alternative drugs.

candidates.reason: Prevalence and trial supported; omit ICD-11 duration and UK availability statements.
Reserve; essential guideline claim (breakthrough fraction and recalculation) not verified from an opened source in this batch.
